Target JAK1/2 loss‑of‑function or beta‑2 microglobulin loss with combination strategies (e.g., epigenetic modulators or cytokine agonists) identified by CrisPRO network analysis. | CrisPRO can simulate pathway rewiring after JAK loss and suggest compensatory targets to restore interferon‑γ signaling. | Speaker noted: "resistant cancers have homozygous JAK1 or JAK2 loss-of-function mutations, or loss of MHC expression by loss of beta‑2 microglobulin."

Identify patients with high circulating beta‑2 integrin‑positive EVs to enrich for those at risk of thrombosis and who may benefit from beta‑2 integrin blockade | CrisPRO can integrate EV proteomic signatures with patient outcomes to generate a predictive classifier for beta‑2 integrin‑positive EV burden | Speaker said: "Clinically, when we measure EVs that express beta‑2 integrin, we can predict which patients in the pancreatic cancer realm are going to form clots"

text: The failure of eEF2 kinase inhibitors due to selectivity issues presents an opportunity to use precision targeting or PROTACs to achieve the selectivity J&J could not. | CrisPRO could identify specific allosteric sites or degradation tags to achieve the selectivity required for eEF2 inhibition in glioblastoma. | never made a drug that was selective enough to go forward to hit this target.

metadata.speaker: Bill Heit
metadata.session_title: Academic Entrepreneurship and Getting Discoveries into Patients, part one: Liftoff

text: The speaker highlights the critical nature of the pre-IND and 'interact' meetings to avoid clinical holds, particularly in cell therapy. | CrisPRO's platform can provide the high-resolution non-clinical safety data (in vitro/in vivo) required to satisfy FDA CMC and safety requirements, reducing the risk of clinical holds. | If your IND goes in and the FDA says, "We're going to put it on a hold," which really just means right now that we see a safety issue here... That's a big no-no from a business aspect of it.

metadata.speaker: Omer Butt
metadata.session_title: Academic Entrepreneurship and Getting Discoveries into Patients, part one: Liftoff

text: The speaker's focus on NK cells and the transition to in vivo CAR-NK suggests a need for better targeting and delivery mechanisms. | CrisPRO's computational spine can optimize the targeting ligands for in vivo CAR-NK delivery to increase specificity and reduce off-target toxicity. | We're now into in vivo, CAR T, CAR NK.

metadata.speaker: Mike Caligiuri
metadata.session_title: Academic Entrepreneurship and Getting Discoveries into Patients, part one: Liftoff

text: Foundation Medicine’s pan‑cancer NGS platform lacks a defined biomarker‑driven use case for early‑stage disease, creating an opening for CrisPRO to provide predictive biomarkers that de‑risk broad diagnostic programs. | CrisPRO can generate robust, AI‑driven biomarker signatures to focus the platform on high‑impact indications, improving trial design and payer acceptance. | Speaker said: "We knew upfront that we wanted to move to commercialization because we knew that you could do the approach in academia. That was happening already. But we felt there was a major gap between the broad utility and what academics could ever supply."

CrisPRO can refine the 80‑gene panel into a minimal, AI‑derived signature linked to a high‑risk population, improving regulatory and payer acceptance. | Use machine‑learning to identify the most predictive subset of genes and generate a validated risk score. | Speaker said: "We had a slide for every gene, literally. I wanted to tell this VC group how excited I was about each and every gene in this biomarker, and the importance."

Implement adaptive trial designs with interim biomarker readouts to de‑risk early‑stage diagnostic development. | CrisPRO can model adaptive designs and predict power for biomarker‑driven endpoints. | Speaker noted the difficulty of raising a second round when first‑round goals were not met.

CrisPRO can analyze transcriptomic and spatial data from treated lesions to identify immune evasion pathways for combinatorial targeting. | Apply AI‑driven pathway deconvolution to generate rational combination hypotheses (e.g., checkpoint blockade). | Speaker admitted limited understanding of why some patients escape: “we don’t fully understand why.”

Develop AI‑derived predictive signatures (e.g., tumor‑infiltrating lymphocyte profile) to enrich future trials. | Machine‑learning on existing trial biospecimens to derive a responder score. | Speaker noted “durable, complete responses… but we need better patient selection.”

CrisPRO can model pathway interactions to prioritize rational combinations and identify biomarkers for patient selection. | Use AI to simulate MEK/KRAS‑G12C/immunotherapy synergy and propose a focused biomarker panel. | Speaker asked: "Do I need to come to them with monotherapy that works? Or can I go to them and say, 'Because we've done this,' and we get a different answer every time."

Lack of readiness-to-quit biomarker could be addressed by CrisPRO predictive modeling to target high‑likelihood quitters. | Use CrisPRO's computational spine to predict individual quit propensity and stratify enrollment. | Speaker said: "Enrolling all patients regardless of readiness to quit, leading to potential dilution of efficacy signal"

metadata.speaker: David Wetter
metadata.institution: University of Utah, Huntsman Cancer Institute

text: Implement adaptive trial designs that balance reach with efficacy endpoints, leveraging CrisPRO's real‑time analytics. | CrisPRO can model expected impact under different reach/efficacy scenarios to optimize design. | Speaker said: "Impact equals reach times efficacy. We think there's way more opportunity increasing reach than efficacy."

metadata.speaker: David Wetter
metadata.institution: University of Utah, Huntsman Cancer Institute

text: CrisPRO could provide digital literacy scoring and predictive modeling to enhance Bridge to Quit enrollment strategies. | Integrate CrisPRO's AI‑driven assessment to identify patients most likely to adopt portal use. | Speaker said: "We know that not everyone has access to patient portals, and this intervention was really aimed at trying to increase the number of people who are on patient portals within the FQHCs."

Use CrisPRO to stratify middle‑school participants by baseline health‑literacy risk to target intensified education. | Apply computational risk scores to personalize curriculum intensity. | Speaker said: "We are assessing if this increased the students' knowledge and intention to gauge in health‑promoting behaviors for themselves."

CrisPRO can model how income changes translate into measurable dietary and screening behavior changes, linking upstream cash to downstream cancer risk. | Apply computational causal inference to quantify pathway from income to colon cancer risk factors. | Speaker said: "Our hypothesis here was the guaranteed income reduces stress and promotes healthier behaviors, and that was the outcome of what we wanted to determine."

Introduce a true no‑intervention control and embed biomarker collection (e.g., cortisol, dietary logs) to strengthen causal claims. | Use CrisPRO's simulation engine to power alternative trial arms and predict required sample sizes for cancer endpoints. | Speaker said: "All participants got money, some got a little less... we will be able to look at the different types."

Identify patients with high tumor CXCL1/2/5/8 chemokine expression to match CXCR2‑armed STAR T cells | Use CrisPRO to develop a CXCR2‑chemokine expression signature for patient selection | Speaker said: "By engineering our STAR T cells to express CXCR2, we effectively created self‑driving T cells"

Target additional antigens beyond GPC3 to prevent antigen‑loss escape | Apply CrisPRO to design multi‑specific CARs or bispecific STAR T constructs | Speaker noted antigen heterogeneity as a barrier to CAR T efficacy

Develop a predictive signature (TFH + intermediate exhausted T‑cell markers) to select patients for TIL therapy | Use CrisPRO to integrate single‑cell transcriptomic signatures into a clinical decision algorithm | Speaker said: "the production quality is more important than the quantity" and highlighted TFH and intermediate exhausted cells as predictive

Engineer TIL manufacturing to enrich TFH and progenitor exhausted subsets (e.g., cytokine cocktails) | Apply CrisPRO to model cytokine/chemokine perturbations that favor desired T‑cell states | Speaker noted that these subsets drive durable immunity

Pair CAR‑DCs with checkpoint blockade to sustain T‑cell activation after DC‑mediated priming | Model synergistic effects of CAR‑DC priming plus PD‑1 inhibition using CrisPRO simulations | Speaker highlighted that CAR‑DCs generate stem‑like T cells in draining lymph nodes

Developing multi-tiered logic-gated ADCs to simulate 'HER2-high' expression levels on targets with lower density | Use computational spine to identify optimal combinatorial target sets and geometric configurations for logic-gated binding | we could create a novel platform that would essentially create combinatorial synthetic targets to behave like HER2 high

metadata.speaker: Felix Hart
metadata.session_title: Advanced Antibody Conjugate and Targeted Therapeutic Platforms

metadata.speaker: Neil O'Brien
metadata.session_title: Advanced Antibody Conjugate and Targeted Therapeutic Platforms

text: Using small bicyclic peptides to achieve rapid tumor penetration and fast renal clearance to widen the therapeutic window | Computational design of high-affinity bicyclic peptides for targets where antibody-based ADCs are too toxic | a very short delivery... enables you really to open that window between efficacy and toxicity

Identify mesothelin‑low or negative clones driving resistance to the CAR T product | CrisPRO can model clonal evolution and suggest combinatorial targets (e.g., EGFR, HER2) to broaden antigen coverage | Speaker hypothesized heterogeneous target expression limits activity

Develop a predictive signature (e.g., baseline CD8/Treg ratio) to select patients likely to benefit from SOX1 knockout | Integrate single‑cell sequencing data to derive a responder classifier | Higher cell dose correlated with response, but no biomarker was used

Develop a combined HLA‑A0201 and ctDNA baseline model to identify patients most likely to benefit | CrisPRO can integrate HLA typing, ctDNA kinetics, and tumor genomics to generate a composite response predictor | Speaker highlighted that ctDNA clearance strongly predicts survival

Design a trial restricting crossover or using ctDNA‑guided continuation to isolate tebentafusp effect | Model crossover impact on survival curves to optimize future trial endpoints | High crossover (86%) confounded OS attribution

Add a randomized atezolizumab/bevacizumab control to quantify RZ001 added benefit | CrisPRO can simulate expected response distributions with and without RZ001 to justify sample size | Speaker acknowledged lack of monotherapy arm
Define quantitative HTERT expression cut‑off predictive of response | Integrate RNA‑scope quantification into a predictive model | All tumors expressed HTERT but response varied

Implement a four‑arm randomized study to dissect contributions of chemotherapy, atezolizumab, and LOAD‑703 | Use CrisPRO to model expected outcomes for each arm and optimize sample size | Speaker acknowledged uncertainty about which component drives benefit

Identify baseline immune signatures (e.g., CD40 expression) predictive of response to LOAD‑703 | Integrate pre‑treatment transcriptomics to predict which tumors will undergo favorable remodeling | Speaker reported massive upregulation of immune biomarkers post‑treatment

Develop next‑generation mRNA TCEs targeting CD20 or CD22 for CD19‑negative relapses | CrisPRO can prioritize alternative antigen‑binding domains based on tumor expression atlases | Audience asked about CD19‑negative patients and alternative targets

Create a predictive model of CD19 density and prior anti‑CD19 therapy to select responders | Integrate flow cytometry and sequencing data to define a response threshold | Speaker noted all patients were CD19‑positive but did not stratify further

Lack of molecular subtyping to select NMIBC patients who will benefit from BCG + IO combinations. | CrisPRO can integrate RNA‑seq subtyping with ctDNA/utDNA to prospectively assign patients to the most effective intravesical or systemic therapy. | Speaker said: "If we had a test that says, 'This patient should get drug X, this one should get drug Y,' that might simplify things a little bit."

Redesign NMIBC BCG‑plus‑IO trials to require baseline molecular subtype and ctDNA/utDNA status. | CrisPRO can simulate trial enrichment strategies using real‑world molecular data to predict power gains. | Speaker noted the need for "new framework for designing clinical trials and what control arms are needed" and highlighted the expense of blanket enrollment.

A3A‑driven DASP state confers multi‑drug resistance via SOX2 up‑regulation. | CrisPRO can predict APOBEC‑driven mutational signatures and flag patients for SOX2‑targeted PROTAC strategies. | Speaker described that A3A exposure leads to FOXM1‑SOX2 axis activation and broad resistance to HER2‑ADC, FGFR3 inhibitors, and EV.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Matthew Galsky
metadata.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

text: Sequential CDK4/6 inhibition sensitizes tumors to ADCs by impairing homologous recombination. | CrisPRO can model CDK4/6‑ADC synergy across genomic contexts to prioritize clinical trials. | Speaker showed that abemaciclib reduced RAD51/TOPBP1 and enhanced ADC cytotoxicity in organoids.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Matthew Galsky
metadata.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

text: Need for integrated blood ctDNA and urine tumor DNA assays to guide adjuvant vs surveillance decisions. | CrisPRO can combine ctDNA and utDNA signals into a composite MRD score for trial enrichment. | Speaker noted that 100% of clinical CR patients had undetectable ctDNA but many had detectable utDNA.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Matthew Galsky
metadata.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

text: Targeting the FOXM1‑SOX2 axis in APOBEC‑high tumors to overcome multi‑drug resistance. | CrisPRO can prioritize SOX2‑degrading compounds and predict which APOBEC‑high patients would benefit. | Speaker demonstrated that SOX2 PROTAC sensitized A3A‑exposed cells to trastuzumab deruxtecan.

Sequential CDK4/6 inhibition followed by ADCs to exploit homologous recombination deficiency. | CrisPRO can simulate timing and dosing of CDK4/6‑ADC combos across genomic backgrounds. | Speaker showed that abemaciclib reduced RAD51/TOPBP1 and enhanced ADC cytotoxicity in organoids.

CHD7 expression defines a subset of NEPC patients with ATR‑checkpoint dependence, but no clinical assay exists. | CrisPRO could develop a CHD7‑based predictive model integrating ATAC‑seq and expression to identify patients likely to respond to ATR‑checkpoint inhibition combined with platinum therapy. | Speaker said: "CHD7 is an early event of the NEPC development" and "knockdown increased sensitivity to cisplatin"

Targeting the CHD7‑ATR axis with checkpoint inhibitors may synergize with cisplatin in NEPC. | CrisPRO can prioritize ATR or CHK1 inhibitors as rational partners for CHD7‑high NEPC based on pathway modeling. | Speaker observed that "combination leads to increased DNA accumulation and also apoptosis" when CHD7 knockdown was paired with cisplatin.

KDM5B inhibitors under development could be repurposed for NEPC if biomarker (KDM5B high / SOX9 activation) stratification is applied. | CrisPRO can integrate KDM5B expression and SOX9 transcriptional signatures to select patients for KDM5B‑targeted trials. | Speaker demonstrated that "KDM5B upregulation could promote NE transformation through activating SOX9" and knockout reduced NE markers.

Combine EZH2 inhibitors with DNMT1 degraders to exploit compensatory epigenetic rewiring in NEPC. | CrisPRO can model synergistic epigenetic network effects to prioritize combination regimens. | Speaker showed that EZH2 deletion caused DNA methylation changes and DNMT1 inhibition led to H3K27 redistribution.

EZH2 inhibitors that failed as monotherapy in NEPC may be rescued by pairing with DNMT1 inhibitors. | CrisPRO can identify patient subsets where EZH2 inhibition restores methylation patterns amenable to DNMT1 blockade. | Speaker noted that "EZH2 is very highly expressed in NEPC" and deletion altered methylome.

UIM‑targeting offers a replication‑independent DNMT1 inhibition strategy that could overcome limitations of 5‑azacytidine. | CrisPRO can benchmark the UIM platform against existing DNMTis using computational binding and off‑target prediction. | Speaker highlighted that "the UIM is essential for DNA methylation maintenance" and that "this approach is not replication‑dependent".

Design early‑phase trials enrolling patients with DNMT1‑UHRF1 axis activation regardless of proliferation rate. | CrisPRO can simulate enrichment strategies based on UHRF1 expression signatures. | Speaker noted that "current DNMTis require replication" whereas the new binders do not.

Existing KDM2A inhibitors could be repurposed for Barrett‑esophagus patients with high KDM2A expression. | CrisPRO can integrate KDM2A expression with enhancer‑acetylation signatures to select candidates for early‑intervention trials. | Speaker showed that "KDM2A overexpression in normal esophageal cells increased oncogenic signaling".

Develop a KDM2A‑high biomarker panel to identify Barrett patients at risk of progression. | CrisPRO can model risk scores using KDM2A levels, H3K36me2 loss, and H3K27ac gain. | Speaker noted a trend of increasing KDM2A from Barrett to EAC and correlation with H3K27ac elevation.

Targeting the KMT2D‑FOXA1‑SOX2 enhancer axis could provide a more precise approach than pan‑H3K4 inhibitors. | CrisPRO can model disruption of the KMT2D‑FOXA1 complex and predict downstream transcriptional collapse in squamous lineage. | Speaker showed physical interaction between KMT2D and FOXA1 and redistribution of MEN1 in KMT2D‑null cells.

MEN1 inhibitor (MI‑503) showed increased sensitivity in KMT2D‑null cells; combining with FOXA1 degraders may enhance efficacy. | CrisPRO can prioritize dual‑target regimens based on synthetic lethality scores. | Speaker reported that "mutant cell lines are more sensitive to this MEN1 inhibitor compared to wild type".

Need for prospective biomarker-driven validation of proteasome inhibitor–induced cardiotoxicity in hematologic cancer survivors | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics and clinical data to identify patients with high proteasome‑inhibitor exposure and predict CVD risk | Speaker said: "we suspect those high risk of developing CVD is treatment induced... proteasome inhibitor treatment group, they have a very high combined score"

Targeting the interferon‑UB subtype with high ubiquitination of DHX9 and AKT1 to overcome poor survival in melanoma | CrisPRO can model ubiquitin‑driven signaling networks to prioritize inhibitors that reverse the hyper‑UB phenotype | Speaker said: "the interferon UB subgroup has a significant worse survival outcomes compared to the other"

Sex‑specific lysosome‑high subtype (GPUMB fucosylation) as a predictive biomarker for therapy response | CrisPRO can integrate glycoproteomics with clinical data to develop sex‑aware predictive models | Speaker noted: "the lysosome high subtype in male tumors had a significantly worse survival, while in female it was neutral or better"

Identify cardioprotective agents (e.g., antihypertensives) that can be co‑prescribed with aromatase inhibitors to mitigate metabolic risk | CrisPRO can predict drug‑drug interaction networks and prioritize safe combination regimens | Speaker highlighted increased hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes with AI adherence

Develop CYP2D6‑guided tamoxifen dosing to improve adherence and reduce unnecessary AI exposure | CrisPRO can integrate genotype‑phenotype models to stratify patients for AI vs tamoxifen | Audience question raised pharmacogenomics as an unaddressed variable

Repurpose proteasome inhibitors for ALT‑positive cancers by combining with PML‑stabilizing agents to achieve selective hyper‑ALT lethality | CrisPRO can model synthetic lethal networks to identify co‑targets that restrict toxicity to ALT cells | Speaker demonstrated that bortezomib induces hyper‑ALT phenotype and cell death in ALT cell lines

Design early‑phase trials enrolling only ALT‑positive tumors with confirmed PML accumulation after proteasome inhibition | CrisPRO can stratify patients based on ALT biomarkers (C‑circles, APBs) for enriched trial cohorts | Speaker highlighted need to test ALT regulation in neuroblastoma, glioma, PANETs

Target stress‑response assembly (gained after vernalstat) to sensitize TNBC to chemotherapy | CrisPRO can predict synergistic drug combinations that disrupt the stress‑response complex | Speaker highlighted a stress response assembly specifically gained in vernalstat‑treated cells

Use loss of SWI/SNF complex as a predictive biomarker for chemotherapy resistance | CrisPRO can integrate complex remodeling signatures to stratify patients likely to respond to specific agents | Speaker noted that the trap‑associated SWI/SNF chromatin regulatory complex is lost in both treatments

Develop a quantitative Trop‑2 expression assay to enrich for responders to ASP2998 | CrisPRO can integrate IHC image analysis with transcriptomics to define expression thresholds predictive of ADC efficacy | Speaker said: "we are not setting a cutoff in the initial trial"

Leverage CrisPRO to model synergistic immune activation from STING agonist and predict optimal dosing schedules | CrisPRO can simulate tumor‑immune dynamics to optimize dual‑payload timing | Speaker highlighted durable immunity and re‑challenge protection mediated by the STING payload

Combine EYA4 inhibition with PARP inhibitors to exploit induced HR deficiency in TNBC | CrisPRO can model synthetic lethal interactions between phosphatase inhibition and PARP blockade | Speaker suggested that EYA4 loss creates HRD phenotype, similar to BRCA loss

Develop methylation‑based assay for EYA4 intron‑exon hypermethylation to select patients for EYA4‑targeted therapy | CrisPRO can integrate epigenetic and expression data to define a predictive biomarker panel | Speaker reported hypermethylation of EYA4 in TNBC correlates with overexpression

Develop a computational connectivity biomarker to select patients with high tumor‑neuron synaptic activity for perampanel therapy | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics connectivity signatures to predict which tumors rely on AMPA‑mediated synapses | Primary endpoints in this trial are basically based on an RNA Seq connectivity score, as well as AI‑based MRI growth dynamics.

Target downstream calcium signaling pathways that sustain proliferation after AMPA blockade | CrisPRO can model calcium‑dependent transcriptional programs to identify combinatorial targets | Synaptic inputs lead to measurable electrophysiological currents that get translated into calcium events in tumor cells.

Incorporate serial ctDNA and functional imaging to monitor emergence of resistance during perampanel treatment | CrisPRO can generate adaptive trial simulations that include dynamic biomarker updates | We need to understand on a really ultra structural basis what really happens when we give patients this perampanel.

Leverage CrisPRO's computational spine to predict selective PKC downstream effectors that disconnect microtubules without global PKC activation | CrisPRO can simulate pathway‑specific PKC modulation to identify narrow‑spectrum compounds | I didn't want to focus on a target that actually kills the cells, but rather, a drug that actually disconnect the cells.

Combine microtubule‑disconnecting agents with standard radiotherapy or temozolomide to exploit radiosensitization | CrisPRO can model synergistic effects of disconnectors with DNA‑damage agents | We designed a platform to find drugs that actually disconnect those networks. Then once they are sensitive we target them with standard of care treatments.

Re‑engineer CCR2 inhibitors with concurrent neutrophil/MPO modulation to prevent compensatory infiltration | CrisPRO can model dual‑target networks to predict synergistic blockade of CCR2 and MPO pathways | Ablating monocytes infiltration led to accelerated neutrophil infiltration.

Develop a spatial MPO‑netosis signature to select patients who may benefit from MPO inhibition | CrisPRO can integrate spatial proteomics and RNA‑seq to generate a predictive MPO activity score | MPO‑deficient tumors showed altered neutrophil phenotype and improved survival.

Baseline myeloid infiltration and EMT signatures predict lack of clinical complete response but were not used for patient selection | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omic spatial data to develop a composite myeloid‑EMT biomarker to enrich future trials for responders | Speaker said: "higher baseline myeloid infiltration was evident in tumor samples from non‑responders"

metadata.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Dana‑Farber Cancer Institute

metadata.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Dana‑Farber Cancer Institute

text: Adaptive enrichment trial enrolling only CCR8‑high tumors and incorporating early on‑treatment biopsies for dynamic Treg/CD8 monitoring | CrisPRO can model adaptive randomization based on early biomarker shifts to optimize dose and patient selection | Speaker admitted lack of clear CCR8‑response relationship and need for more homogeneous populations

metadata.speaker: Bruno Boccorni
metadata.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Dana‑Farber Cancer Institute

text: Integration of EMT, metabolic, and lineage plasticity signatures to stratify patients for combination therapies | CrisPRO can combine bulk and single‑cell RNA‑seq with spatial profiling to generate a composite EMT‑Metabolic resistance score for trial enrichment | Speaker said: "Acquired resistance was associated with upregulation of EMT and metabolic pathways"

metadata.speaker: Archana Balan
metadata.institution: Johns Hopkins University / Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center

text: Targeting the FGF/mTOR proliferative signaling axis enriched in acquired resistance | CrisPRO can prioritize FGF/mTOR inhibitors as rational combination partners with PD‑1 blockade in the identified genomic subset | Speaker noted enrichment of mutations in the FGF and mTOR pathways in the acquired resistance group

metadata.speaker: Archana Balan
metadata.institution: Johns Hopkins University / Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center

text: Prospective longitudinal sampling (paired pre‑/post‑IO biopsies) to capture dynamic evolution of EMT and immune states | CrisPRO can simulate adaptive trial designs that trigger combination escalation when EMT signatures rise | Speaker acknowledged that "the study used unmatched pre‑ and post‑IO samples"

metadata.speaker: Archana Balan
metadata.institution: Johns Hopkins University / Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center

text: Mechanical confinement induces chromatin de‑compaction and creates new transcriptional hubs that drive metastasis; CrisPRO could model these chromatin changes to predict which tumors will acquire a mesenchymal, highly deformable phenotype. | CrisPRO's computational spine can integrate ATAC‑seq, Hi‑C and histone‑mark data to forecast chromatin hub formation and identify patients at risk of mechanical‑stress‑driven dissemination. | Speaker said: "migration through these narrow channels induces the repression of heterochromatin and also reduces the density of the nucleus... this endows much more physical nuclear deformability"

Many failed Phase 3 trials lacked baseline IFN‑γ / PD‑L1 stratification; CrisPRO could provide a predictive resistance model (NeoPredict) to enrich future trials. | CrisPRO can integrate transcriptomic, DNA and clinical features to generate a resistance score for patient selection. | Speaker said: "the anti‑TIGIT trial showed a trend for poorer survival, likely because we did not look at baseline tissue before making the decision."

Low-dose ipilimumab in CheckMate 915 diluted efficacy; CrisPRO could simulate dose‑response curves to optimize checkpoint dosing before trial launch. | CrisPRO's computational modeling of immune activation can predict optimal checkpoint dosing regimens. | Speaker said: "we know that ipilimumab, not PD‑1, has a dose‑response relationship, higher dose, better response."

Third‑space patients identified by NeoPredict could be matched with emerging CAR‑T or TIL platforms; CrisPRO can prioritize antigen targets (e.g., TYRP1, IL‑13Rα2) based on expression heterogeneity. | CrisPRO can rank surface antigens for CAR design using tumor‑specific expression and splice‑variant data. | Speaker said: "we have a suite of prediction tools... NeoPredict predicts resistance to PD‑1 monotherapy."

Use of lymphatic fluid from surgical drains dramatically increases ctDNA yield and improves risk stratification for patients who are ctDNA‑negative in plasma. | CrisPRO can integrate lymphatic‑fluid‑derived cfDNA sequencing with its computational spine to generate a high‑sensitivity MRD signature, overcoming plasma‑only limitations. | Speaker said: "lymph ctDNA MRD was associated with worse PFS... lymph ctDNA outperformed individual pathology features... lymph ctDNA 24 h significantly stratified progression‑free survival, while plasma did not at this early time point."

Spatial ecotype inference from cfDNA methylation provides a non‑invasive readout of the tumor microenvironment, a capability not offered by standard ctDNA mutation panels. | CrisPRO’s AI‑driven methylation deconvolution can be extended to predict spatial ecotypes, giving a competitive edge over mutation‑only assays. | Speaker said: "we developed a binary neural network to infer spatial ecotypes from plasma cfDNA methylomes and predict immunotherapy response."

Incorporate baseline tumor fraction or shedding biomarkers into enrollment criteria for ctDNA‑adaptive trials to enrich for patients where MRD detection is feasible. | CrisPRO can model shedding probability per tumor type and recommend stratified enrollment thresholds. | Speaker said: "we need to know the concordance between ctDNA MRD positivity and outcomes… we do not have that answer, which motivated the Tic‑Tac‑Toe trial."

Develop cfDNA methylation‑based spatial ecotype signatures to capture microenvironment‑driven resistance that mutation‑only assays miss. | CrisPRO’s methylation deconvolution pipeline can generate ecotype scores from low‑VAF cfDNA, providing a complementary resistance biomarker. | Speaker highlighted that "a significant fraction of ctDNA‑negative patients still recur" suggesting non‑mutational mechanisms.

CrisPRO can combine MAESTRO‑derived ultra‑low VAF mutation data with its computational spine to improve variant calling confidence at part‑per‑million levels. | CrisPRO’s error‑modeling framework can further suppress residual noise, extending MAESTRO’s sensitivity. | Speaker said: "MAESTRO converts low VAF mutations to high VAF mutations to detect ctDNA at or below part per million levels with high specificity."

text: Need for molecular biomarkers that distinguish the three CT‑based cachexia subtypes (A, B, C) to enable targeted interventions | CrisPRO can integrate longitudinal imaging features with multi‑omics to derive predictive signatures for each anatomical subtype | We arrived at three pretty clean clusters of data... type A patients have progressive increases in spleen and liver volume and do the worst overall survival

P53 mutations are strongly associated with higher risk of cachexia across cancers | CrisPRO can prioritize P53‑driven pathways and suggest combinatorial targets to mitigate cachexia in P53‑mutant tumors | When you do this across diseases, you find many genomic correlates of risk of cachexia, and the clear smoking gun is P53

High‑symptom burden cluster shows elevated GDF15 and inflammatory markers; need a predictive biomarker panel to prospectively assign patients to subtypes | CrisPRO can develop a multi‑modal classifier (clinical, lab, imaging) to stratify patients before therapy | Patients with higher symptom burden are higher rates of elevation in GDF15 in the serum as well as higher inflammatory markers like IL6 and IL8

Future interventional trials should enroll patients based on biomarker‑defined subtypes rather than all‑comers | CrisPRO can simulate enrichment strategies and estimate power gains from biomarker‑guided enrollment | Current trials (e.g., ROMANA, POWER, olanzapine) use a one‑size‑fits‑all approach despite evidence of distinct cachexia phenotypes

Targeting tumor‑derived PGE2 production (e.g., PTGES or PTGS2 inhibition) may reverse cachexia and improve checkpoint inhibitor efficacy | CrisPRO can prioritize small‑molecule or CRISPR‑based strategies to suppress PGE2 synthesis and model downstream effects on immune activation | Knockdown of PTGES prevents or delays the onset of cachexia in KRAS/LKB1 mice; PTGS2 knockout protects C26 mice from weight loss

Combine PGE2 pathway inhibition with anti‑PD‑L1 therapy to overcome resistance in cachectic patients | CrisPRO can simulate combination efficacy and predict synergistic biomarkers for trial design | Cachectic mice show poor response to anti‑PD‑L1; PGE2‑high tumors have elevated neutrophil and macrophage suppressive populations

CrisPRO’s integrative modeling of microbiome, myeloid cell states, and prostaglandin signaling offers a unique angle not addressed by existing pipelines | Leverage multi‑omics integration to identify patients where microbiome‑driven PGE2 is a dominant driver of cachexia | Dysbiosis in tumor microenvironment correlates with neutrophil infiltration and higher PGE2 production

Need for robust, AI‑derived confounder extraction from EHRs to enable accurate propensity‑score adjustment in hybrid control trials. | CrisPRO’s computational spine can integrate LLM‑extracted covariates with validated causal models to improve propensity‑score weighting and reduce bias. | Speaker said: "advances in AI, especially LLMs, do hold the potential to unlock additional confounder information from the EHR"

Demonstrated high‑reliability LLM extraction of progression events suggests a platform where CrisPRO could provide calibrated uncertainty metrics for AI‑derived endpoints. | CrisPRO can overlay Bayesian confidence intervals on LLM‑derived survival curves to flag potential hallucinations. | Speaker said: "LLM‑extracted data, it looks like single curves on each of these plots, but they're actually two curves that are superimposed"

Integrate CrisPRO’s dynamic borrowing framework to weight prospective real‑world control data based on similarity metrics, reducing bias from missing covariates. | CrisPRO can compute similarity scores in real time and adjust borrowing weights, allowing inclusion of incomplete registries while preserving type I error control. | Speaker said: "the prospective model yields an expected data quality over 85% capture of the key variables" but also noted missing PRO and SDH data

Add automated extraction of molecular biomarker status from EHR (e.g., EGFR mutation) to enable biomarker‑selected analyses within the prospective registry. | CrisPRO’s LLM pipeline can reliably extract genomic test results and feed them into propensity models. | Speaker highlighted that the trial design lacked biomarker stratification in the real‑world arm.

TCL1A expression could serve as a biomarker to identify high‑risk CHIP clones for targeted intervention. | CrisPRO can integrate genomic and epigenomic data to predict TCL1A‑driven clonal fitness and prioritize patients for TCL1A‑targeted therapies. | Speaker said: "we think TCL1A might actually be a very good therapeutic target because you might predict that you'd be able to block its function without really affecting normal tissues very much."

Existing drugs that modulate AKT signaling may be repurposed to counteract TCL1A‑mediated AKT activation in CHIP. | CrisPRO can model pathway dependencies and suggest AKT‑targeted agents that could mitigate TCL1A‑driven expansion. | Speaker described TCL1A binding to the PH domain of AKT and potentially activating AKT via an unknown mechanism.

PACER fitness estimates could be incorporated into CrisPRO to stratify patients for surveillance or preventive trials. | CrisPRO can combine PACER‑derived fitness scores with other omics to predict high‑risk clones. | Speaker described the PACER method to infer clonal expansion rates from passenger mutation counts.

metadata.speaker: Jyoti Nangalia
metadata.institution: Cambridge University Hospital / Wellcome Sanger Institute

text: Design trials that enroll participants based on smoking status and PACER‑derived fitness to test anti‑TCL1A therapies. | CrisPRO can model expected effect sizes for interventions in sub‑cohorts defined by smoking and fitness metrics. | Speaker highlighted smoking as the only measured environmental factor positively associated with clonal expansion.

metadata.speaker: Jyoti Nangalia
metadata.institution: Cambridge University Hospital / Wellcome Sanger Institute

metadata.speaker: Ben Ebert

metadata.speaker: Ben Ebert
metadata.institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School

text: Combine IL‑1β blockade with ACLY inhibition to achieve synergistic reduction of inflammation in TET2‑mutant CHIP. | CrisPRO can simulate combination effects on inflammatory readouts and predict optimal dosing schedules. | Speaker noted that IL‑1β inhibition reverses phenotype but metabolic defects persist.

metadata.speaker: Ben Ebert
metadata.institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School

text: Partner with CrisPRO to add mechanistic validation layers to generative models to address blindspots. | CrisPRO can provide computational validation against known pathways and resistance mechanisms. | Speaker highlighted that generative models lack clear regulatory pathways and validation.

metadata.speaker: Jeffrey Leake
metadata.institution: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center / Synthesize Bio

text: Use CrisPRO to generate explainable surrogate biomarkers that satisfy FDA’s fit‑for‑purpose validation without full explainability. | CrisPRO can produce transparent mechanistic maps linking image features to molecular alterations. | Speaker emphasized that explainability may not be required but fit‑for‑purpose validation is essential.

Incorporate CrisPRO‑validated biomarkers into trial enrollment criteria to avoid dilution of signal. | CrisPRO can identify high‑confidence patient subgroups for targeted enrollment. | Speaker warned that broad enrollment without biomarker selection dilutes signal.

Develop public reference datasets for AI model external validation as urged by FDA. | CrisPRO can curate and host standardized oncology datasets for community benchmarking. | Speaker called for public reference data sets for benchmarking AI models in oncology.

metadata.speaker: Jeevan Puthenvedu
metadata.institution: FDA CDER / Oncology Center of Excellence

text: Incorporate a human‑in‑the‑loop safety check alongside AI risk stratification to reduce model influence. | CrisPRO can provide decision‑support dashboards that flag high‑risk predictions for reviewer oversight. | Speaker discussed model influence and decision consequence as key risk factors.

metadata.speaker: Jeevan Puthenvedu
metadata.institution: FDA CDER / Oncology Center of Excellence

text: Identify GBM patients with high CD8+ T cell DPP4 expression who may benefit from repurposed DPP4 inhibitors. | CrisPRO can integrate single‑cell RNA‑seq and metabolomic data to predict which tumors have DPP4‑high exhausted CD8 T cells and model responder likelihood. | Speaker said: we observed that CD8 T cells are the main expressers of DPP4 and that inhibition improves proliferation and cytotoxicity.

Repurpose FDA‑approved gliptins (e.g., sitagliptin) for GBM by combining with checkpoint blockade or CAR‑T therapy. | CrisPRO can simulate drug‑target engagement in the GBM microenvironment and predict synergistic dosing schedules with PD‑1 blockade. | Speaker said: we turned into the Medicare data set and performed a retrospective analysis where we looked for the patients who were on DPP4 inhibitors and observed better outcomes.

Develop a computational switch model to predict optimal timing of GLUT3 induction based on tumor glucose measurements. | CrisPRO can integrate real‑time glucose sensor data with CAR‑T activation kinetics to design inducible GLUT3 promoters. | Speaker said: on‑demand GLUT3 expression enabled glucose uptake only after antigen recognition and avoided toxicity.

Combine on‑demand GLUT3 CAR T cells with checkpoint blockade to further reduce PD‑1/TIM‑3 upregulation. | CrisPRO can model synergistic effects of metabolic enhancement plus PD‑1 inhibition on T‑cell exhaustion trajectories. | Speaker said: stable GLUT3‑expressing CAR T cells showed high PD‑1/TIM‑3 expression, whereas on‑demand did not.

Rescue A20‑targeted ACTs by focusing on zinc‑finger‑7 editing rather than full knockout. | CrisPRO can predict off‑target editing outcomes and model the impact of zinc‑finger‑7 disruption on T‑cell signaling networks. | Speaker said: zinc finger seven targeting greatly enhanced ACT activity, whereas full A20 knockout was less effective.

Combine zinc‑finger‑7 edited ACT with RIP3 or caspase‑1 modulators to further boost perforin degranulation. | CrisPRO can simulate synergistic effects of dual pathway modulation on degranulation kinetics. | Speaker said: RIP3 ablation nearly eliminated the tumor phenotype in zinc finger seven mice, indicating a non‑canonical pathway.

Use galectin‑1 expression on CD8 T cells as a biomarker to select patients for combination therapy with LAG‑3 or VISTA inhibitors. | CrisPRO can integrate single‑cell RNA‑seq and glycoproteomics to predict galectin‑1‑high exhausted T‑cell subsets. | Speaker said: galectin‑1 expression increases during T cell exhaustion and binds LAG‑3/VISTA.

Develop small‑molecule or antibody blockers of the galectin‑1/LAG‑3/VISTA interaction to complement existing checkpoint blockade. | CrisPRO can model the structural interface and prioritize compounds that disrupt the glycan‑dependent interaction. | Speaker said: galectin‑1 binds LAG‑3 and VISTA with measurable affinity, and this binding is glycan‑dependent.

Design combination trials that pair PTPN2 inhibition with SOCS3 modulation to sustain IL‑2/STAT5 signaling. | CrisPRO can model cytokine milieu dynamics and predict optimal dosing schedules for dual inhibition. | Speaker said: double knockout PTPN2 and SOCS3 showed strong levels of IL‑2/STAT5 compared to single knockouts.

metadata.speaker: Yaita Senat
metadata.institution: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard

text: Target SOCS3 upregulation as a resistance node to PTPN2‑based metabolic reprogramming. | CrisPRO can simulate SOCS3 knockdown effects on STAT5 phosphorylation kinetics. | Speaker said: SOCS3 is a known inhibitor of JAK‑STAT pathway and is induced in PTPN2‑inhibited T cells.

metadata.speaker: Yaita Senat
metadata.institution: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard

text: Target the arsenic‑binding cysteine triad mutations in PML‑RAR to restore arsenic sensitivity | CrisPRO can model the structural impact of cysteine triad mutations and design small molecules that bind alternative sites to induce degradation | mutations of the alpha helix that allows the formation of this trimer ... were found in a tri‑resistant APL

Combine retinoic acid/arsenic with agents that boost p53 activation to enhance senescence‑driven cure | CrisPRO can predict synergistic p53‑activating compounds that complement the existing regimen | degradation of PML‑RER allows reformation of PML nuclear bodies, which will drive p53 activation, loss of self‑renewal senescence

Implement CrisPRO‑derived apoptotic priming scores to stratify patients for BCL2 family inhibitor trials | CrisPRO can integrate BH3 profiling data with genomic features to generate a predictive priming index | baseline priming correlates with chemotherapy sensitivity across cancer types

Combine BCL‑XL degraders (e.g., DT2216) with standard chemotherapy in unprimed solid tumors | CrisPRO can predict synergistic drug pairs that raise priming above a therapeutic threshold | BCL‑XL inhibitor plus vincristine rescued response in adult rhabdomyosarcoma model

Use CrisPRO to develop an NF1‑based predictive model for maytansinoid ADC response | CrisPRO can integrate NF1 mutation, expression, and microtubule dynamics data to generate a response score for ADCs | NF1 knockout cells responded much, much better to the same drug; patient data showed longer PFS in NF1‑mutated cohort

Rescue maytansinoid ADC programs that failed in unselected trials by re‑designing them for NF1‑mutant populations | CrisPRO can identify sub‑populations with high predicted priming for microtubule repair deficiency | clinical cohort showed significant PFS benefit in NF1‑mutated patients

Need for better stratification of MCED sensitivity by cancer stage and size to improve predictive performance. | CrisPRO can model stage‑specific shedding signatures to predict assay sensitivity across tumor sizes. | Speaker said: "Statistical power is a critical issue here. And there's little data on program sensitivity."

metadata.speaker: Bob Smith
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Incorporate prospective cohort designs with serial ctDNA sampling to capture program sensitivity. | CrisPRO can simulate longitudinal sampling schedules to optimize trial power for program sensitivity endpoints. | Speaker said: "We have not had an opportunity to look at the performance of these tests very often when they've been done year after year."

metadata.speaker: Bob Smith
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Develop computational models to predict CSO accuracy across tumor subtypes where empirical data are sparse. | CrisPRO can integrate methylation signatures with tissue‑of‑origin classifiers to improve CSO predictions. | Speaker said: "Across multiple data sets, cancer signal origin is accurate enough to be clinically useful as a workup diagnostic tool"

metadata.speaker: Nima Visvade
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Create a framework to map biologic families (e.g., HPV‑related tumors) to shared CSO pathways. | CrisPRO can cluster tumors by shared epigenetic signatures to define biologic parity groups. | Speaker said: "Some CSOs reflect embryologic, molecular, or histologic relationships more so than strict organ boundaries"

metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Incorporate age‑sex standardization prospectively in trial protocols to avoid post‑hoc adjustments. | CrisPRO can simulate population distributions to guide enrollment quotas before trial launch. | Speaker said: "We adjusted it, and then we said, 'Okay, how does the performance of the test change?'"

metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Provide a standardized computational framework to assess verification bias across MCED trials. | CrisPRO can generate bias‑adjusted performance estimates using simulated verification pathways. | Speaker said: "There are statistical techniques to deal with these biases, however"

metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Partner with CrisPRO to create decision‑support tools that triage positive MCED results to appropriate local or regional diagnostic resources. | CrisPRO can generate referral algorithms based on CSO and local resource availability. | Speaker said: "Being able to have a lifeline to the tertiary academic center to escalate signal positives"

metadata.speaker: Gary Puckrein
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests

text: Peak gait cadence and activity fragmentation predict survival independent of ECOG and step count, suggesting a novel prognostic biomarker that CrisPRO could model and validate across larger cohorts. | CrisPRO can integrate continuous wearable metrics with clinical covariates to develop a composite prognostic score and test its predictive power in multi‑institutional datasets. | Speaker said: "only peak gait cadence and activity fragmentation remained significant after adjusting for age, cancer stage, type, ECOG, and step count"

metadata.speaker: Carissa (Karissa) Lo
metadata.institution: University of Pittsburgh and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center

text: Low activity fragmentation is associated with higher mortality, indicating a possible physiologic resistance pathway (frailty) that could be targeted with interventions. | CrisPRO’s AI can identify patients with high fragmentation and recommend tailored exercise or supportive care programs to mitigate frailty‑related resistance. | Speaker said: "patients that had more fragmented activity in the yellow had greater mortality over the follow‑up"

metadata.speaker: Carissa (Karissa) Lo
metadata.institution: University of Pittsburgh and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center

text: Future trials could stratify enrollment by baseline gait cadence to avoid signal dilution from low‑risk patients. | CrisPRO can simulate trial power under different stratification schemes using existing wearable datasets to optimize design. | Speaker said: "these gait cadence and activity fragmentation measures might be capturing something independent of what clinicians can perceive"

metadata.speaker: Carissa (Karissa) Lo
metadata.institution: University of Pittsburgh and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center

text: The retrospective analysis shows that wearable‑derived metrics have prognostic value even when traditional clinical endpoints are modest; CrisPRO could repurpose existing wearable data to rescue underperforming biomarkers. | Apply CrisPRO’s multimodal modeling to re‑analyze legacy trial data with wearable streams, potentially revealing hidden efficacy signals. | Speaker said: "we found that step count did predict survival, but peak gait cadence and activity fragmentation were stronger"

metadata.speaker: Carissa (Karissa) Lo
metadata.institution: University of Pittsburgh and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center

text: CrisPRO can provide a unified, oncology‑focused analytics layer on top of heterogeneous wearable streams, addressing the current reliance on generic open‑source pipelines. | Deploy CrisPRO’s proprietary modeling to harmonize data across Fitbit, Apple Watch, Garmin, and Oura without costly third‑party aggregators. | Speaker said: "there are a number of companies out there that are data aggregators, ... they are kind of expensive"

Incorporate multi‑day physiological change criteria and disease‑specific thresholds (e.g., for immunotherapy‑related toxicity) into digital trial protocols. | CrisPRO can simulate different alert windows and optimize sensitivity/specificity for oncology endpoints such as cytokine release syndrome. | Speaker said: "we usually waited at least a couple of days, and we look at changes in resting heart rate and in at least one between sleep and physical activity before triggering an alarm"

Partner with oncology groups to embed CrisPRO analytics into remote monitoring of checkpoint inhibitor trials, leveraging the foundation model concept. | Use CrisPRO’s foundation model fine‑tuned on oncology patients to predict irAE risk from wearable data. | Speaker said: "the idea is really to study the individual, ... and then trigger changes with respect to this normal"

Integrate CrisPRO’s multimodal AI platform with existing RPM workflows to provide actionable risk scores (e.g., early decompensation, irAE prediction) that address clinician alert fatigue. | CrisPRO can aggregate wearable, PRO, and EMR data into a single risk dashboard with configurable alert thresholds. | Speaker said: "we need a layer of artificial intelligence in order to make these continuous results interpretable"

Design oncology RPM trials that stratify patients by digital literacy and baseline activity, and include objective wearable endpoints alongside PROs. | Use CrisPRO simulations to estimate power under different stratification schemes before launching the trial. | Speaker said: "most patients aren't health literate, can't really do digital health things"

Demonstrate that AI‑derived performance‑status scores from wearables outperform physician estimates in predicting survival, providing a competitive advantage over current RPM solutions. | Validate CrisPRO’s gait‑based performance metrics against ECOG/Karnofsky in a prospective cohort. | Speaker said: "physicians are only right 40% of the time"

GRB2 inhibitor induces cGAS‑STING activation via replication stress; CrisPRO could model this innate immune activation to predict combinatorial partners | Use CrisPRO's pathway simulation to identify synergistic immune checkpoint or STING agonist combos | Speaker said: inhibitor increases gamma H2AX and activates cGAS‑STING pathway

No biomarker used to select tumors dependent on GRB2 dimerization | Apply CrisPRO's predictive modeling to discover expression signatures of GRB2 dependency | Speaker noted specificity concerns due to many SH2/SH3 proteins

If plexin B2 antibodies fail due to target loss, CrisPRO can repurpose the AI pipeline to design antibodies against the up‑regulated DL3 target | Leverage existing antibody language model to rapidly generate DL3‑specific candidates | Speaker identified DL3 up‑regulation in plexin B2‑low neuroendocrine clusters

Lack of prospective biomarker to select patients with high plexin B2‑cluster activity | Develop CrisPRO‑derived predictive signature integrating CTC‑cluster transcriptomics | Speaker noted plexin B2 enrichment in CTC clusters but no clinical assay described

Identify patients with high SWELL‑1/LRRC8C expression to enrich for responders | Use CrisPRO to integrate TCGA expression and metabolomics to generate a predictive score | Speaker noted ~1‑fold increase of SWELL‑1 expression in IDH mutant tumors from TCGA

Model compensatory up‑regulation of alternative LRRC8 subunits that may bypass SWELL‑1 inhibition | Simulate channel subunit composition dynamics to design combination strategies | Speaker observed AD knockdown increased D‑2HG release via AC channel formation

Combine eIF4A1 inhibition with MCL1 inhibitors to exploit synthetic lethality | CrisPRO can prioritize dosing schedules for synergistic combos | Speaker identified MCL1 as top sensitizer in CRISPR screen

metadata.institution: Beckman Research Institute of the City of Hope

text: Identify AML subsets with high free eIF4A1/YB‑1 complex activity | Use CrisPRO to develop a transcriptomic signature predicting response to zoledronate | Speaker showed YB‑1 interaction drives PHGDH mRNA stability

metadata.speaker: Xiaoxu Zhang
metadata.institution: Beckman Research Institute of the City of Hope

text: Combine anti‑Rho2 with APR‑246 (p53 reactivator) to exploit redox vulnerability | CrisPRO can model redox network to predict optimal dosing ratios | Speaker showed anti‑Rho2 lowers NRF2 targets and sensitizes cells to APR‑246

Develop assay to quantify surface Rho2 on patient tumors for enrollment | Leverage CrisPRO to translate CITE‑seq signatures into a clinical IHC panel | Speaker used CITE‑seq to identify Rho2‑positive cells

Use SLC7A11 expression to select patients likely to respond to thiostrepton | CrisPRO can integrate RNA‑seq and proteomics to build a predictive response model | Speaker identified SLC7A11 up‑regulation in non‑responding explants

Develop next‑generation PRDX3 inhibitors with improved solubility and selectivity using AI‑driven scaffold optimization | Apply CrisPRO's generative chemistry module to design covalent warheads specific for PRDX3 active site cysteines | Speaker mentioned ongoing SAR to reduce off‑target effects

Identify biomarkers (e.g., KMT2A rearrangement, FLT3 mutation) that predict OT-82 + venetoclax response | Use CrisPRO to model metabolic dependencies and predict responders | Speaker noted higher response in KMT2A‑rearranged and FLT3‑mutated PDXs but lacked statistical significance

Combine OT-82 with agents that mitigate thrombocytopenia | Predict synergistic combos that spare platelets via pathway analysis | Speaker mentioned need for clinical protocols that mitigate thrombocytopenia

Target AP‑1 driven persistor program to sustain CAR T activity | Model transcription factor network to identify small‑molecule inhibitors of AP‑1 that could prevent persistor formation | Speaker highlighted AP‑1 genes (JunB, FosB) high in persistor cells

Develop assay for early persistor signature to select patients for combination therapy | Use CrisPRO to integrate single‑cell data and predict persistor emergence | Speaker noted persistor cells arise from multiple early states and correlate with durable response

Apply CrisPRO to redesign KatTCIP linkers for stronger ternary complex formation | Predict optimal linker geometry to increase cooperativity | Speaker noted limited plasticity of ligand binding and only two neo‑hydrogen bonds
Combine TCIP3 with MYC inhibitors to overcome residual MYC activity | Model network to identify synergistic targets | Speaker reported residual MYC expression despite BCL6 activation

Develop a gene‑expression signature for FGFR1‑positive CAFs to select patients for FGFRi + CAR‑T | Use CrisPRO to integrate scRNA‑seq CAF data and predict responders | Speaker highlighted that only mesenchymal microenvironment tumors responded

Combine FGFRi with agents that boost macrophage recruitment (e.g., CSF1R agonists) | Model cytokine network to identify synergistic combos | FGFR inhibition increased MCP chemokines and macrophage infiltration

Develop YTHDC1 inhibitor or degrader to prevent condensate‑mediated resistance | Model condensate dynamics to predict optimal dosing schedules | Speaker demonstrated that YTHDC1 inhibition reverses resistance in vitro

Use YTHDC1 expression/condensate liquid‑like score to select patients for METTL3 inhibitor therapy | Integrate imaging data with CrisPRO to generate predictive biomarker | Speaker highlighted correlation between condensate properties and drug response

Develop assay for TRAF2 deficiency to identify AML patients likely to respond | Model TRAF2 network to predict responders | Speaker showed TRAF2 repression across AML subtypes correlates with sensitivity
Combine lymphotoxin‑α with agents that further down‑regulate TRAF2 or enhance necroptosis | Predict synergistic combos targeting necroptosis | Speaker noted necroptosis pathway involvement

Explore MET12L as a therapeutic target to mitigate thrombocytosis in MPN patients | Model mediator complex alterations to design small molecules that mimic MET12L loss | Speaker showed MET12L deletion counteracts thrombocytosis in JAK2‑V617F mice

Develop MET12L expression assay to identify patients with high platelet counts | Integrate scRNA‑seq with CrisPRO to predict high‑MET12L responders | Single‑cell RNA‑seq data linked MET12L expression to platelet features in MPN/MDS patients

Need for robust primary resistance biomarkers (e.g., lncRNA‑EGFR isoform D, lineage‑plastic signatures) to enrich trials. | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omics (RNA‑seq, spatial transcriptomics, proteomics) to generate predictive signatures for primary resistance. | Speaker noted primary resistance remains poorly understood and that 50‑60% of frontline third‑gen EGFR patients lack any known resistance mechanism on NGS.

Target lineage‑plastic and stromal‑rich tumor microenvironment (myeloid‑skewed) using FAP‑directed or radioligand therapies. | CrisPRO can model tumor‑stroma interaction networks to prioritize combination partners that reverse myeloid‑skewed states. | Speaker described a stromal‑rich TME associated with poor‑risk relapse and suggested FAP‑targeting drugs as potential combos.

Incorporate on‑treatment biopsies and ctDNA monitoring to dynamically adapt therapy, reducing dilution of signal in broad Phase III studies. | CrisPRO can provide real‑time decision algorithms linking ctDNA kinetics to recommended combination switches. | Speaker advocated single‑agent third‑gen TKI with on‑treatment biopsy to allocate combination agents, noting current trials lack such adaptive design.

AI‑driven analysis of spatial omics and pathology could provide the molecular biomarkers needed to stratify patients within the eco‑evolutionary framework. | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑modal spatial data to generate predictive microenvironment signatures for patient selection. | Speaker highlighted that "tumor microenvironment grammar" is key to understanding response and that current companion biomarkers (PD‑L1, TMB) are insufficient.

Modeling niche‑construction feedback loops with generative AI could identify novel intervention points to break clonal dominance. | CrisPRO’s probabilistic modeling can simulate evolutionary trajectories and test interventions that alter selective pressures. | Speaker described how harsh TME conditions create steep fitness gradients that drive monoclonal dominance.

Use AI‑generated virtual patient cohorts to refine eligibility criteria and power calculations before launching real trials. | CrisPRO can simulate trial arms with mechanistic tumor‑microenvironment models to predict enrichment strategies. | Speaker described how TrialScope can instantly recalculate eligibility numbers when criteria change.

Partner with AI platform to integrate spatial proteomics (GigaTime) predictions into biomarker‑driven combination strategies. | CrisPRO can fuse predicted spatial proteomics with drug response models to prioritize combination regimens. | Speaker presented GigaTime translating H&E slides into virtual multiplex immunofluorescence maps.

Leverage CrisPRO’s generative patient‑journey modeling to address confounding limitations of current real‑world AI models. | CrisPRO incorporates causal inference layers to explicitly adjust for hidden confounders in virtual trial simulations. | Speaker acknowledged that observational data are subject to confounders and that AI must model unknown confounders.

Develop a CrisPRO‑driven predictive model that integrates the 23‑gene expression signature with spatial immune checkpoint data to better stratify patients at risk of metastasis. | CrisPRO can combine bulk transcriptomic signatures with spatially resolved checkpoint ligand expression to generate a composite risk score. | Speaker said: "we do not have high‑quality biomarkers to predict who will progress to metastatic disease"

metadata.speaker: Li Ding
metadata.session_title: Decoding Tumor Evolution through the Human Tumor Atlas Network

metadata.speaker: Li Ding
metadata.session_title: Decoding Tumor Evolution through the Human Tumor Atlas Network

metadata.speaker: Irene Ghobrial
metadata.session_title: Decoding Tumor Evolution through the Human Tumor Atlas Network

text: Rescue early‑stage CAR‑T programs by selecting patients with high MST scores who are likely to benefit from immunotherapy before overt disease. | CrisPRO can simulate CAR‑T efficacy across MST‑defined risk strata to prioritize trial enrollment. | Speaker said: "we showed 100% MRD‑negative responses in early smoldering myeloma patients treated with CAR‑T"

metadata.speaker: Irene Ghobrial
metadata.session_title: Decoding Tumor Evolution through the Human Tumor Atlas Network

text: Develop a computational model to predict organoid establishment success from biopsy histology and molecular data, enabling pre‑selection of patients likely to benefit from PDO testing. | CrisPRO can integrate imaging, genomic, and clinical features to generate a predictive score for PDO success, reducing trial dilution. | Speaker said: "We want to be 80%, 90%... we fail a lot" and "the patients with better outcomes, we can't make the organoids"

Apply high‑content imaging‑based rapid pharmacotyping (30‑day readout) to replace ATP‑based assays, increasing throughput and reducing time‑to‑result. | CrisPRO’s image‑analysis pipeline can automate feature extraction and predict drug response faster than traditional assays. | Speaker demonstrated a microscopy‑based assay with correlation coefficient comparable to ATP readout and a median 30‑day turnaround.

Use CrisPRO to model protein‑synthesis‑driven resistance in monocytic AML and predict combinatorial partners that overcome venetoclax resistance. | CrisPRO can simulate pathway flux changes and prioritize CDK4/6 or other inhibitors to counteract the resistance node. | Speaker highlighted that monocyte‑like cells resist venetoclax via protein synthesis up‑regulation.

Incorporate cell‑state biomarkers into future BEAT‑AML trials to stratify patients and reduce signal dilution. | CrisPRO can generate a composite cell‑state score for each patient to guide arm allocation. | Speaker noted that differentiation state governs response for 73 of 120 drugs tested.

Develop a CrisPRO‑driven multi‑omics signature that combines CSC flow data with transcriptomics to better define resistant subpopulations. | CrisPRO can integrate flow cytometry, RNA‑seq, and drug response to generate a refined predictive model. | Speaker noted that "the less malignant cultures need more care and consideration" and that CSC markers are nonspecific.

Identify agents that specifically sensitize CSC‑enriched populations (e.g., protein synthesis inhibitors) to improve ChemoID‑guided regimens. | CrisPRO can simulate microenvironment‑modulated drug response and prioritize combos that overcome fibroblast‑mediated resistance. | Speaker showed that fibroblasts increase drug resistance and that certain drugs are impervious to microenvironment effects.

Need for computational models to stratify reduced penetrance BRCA variants beyond binary ClinVar labels | CrisPRO can integrate functional assay scores with population data to generate quantitative risk scores for hypomorphic variants | Speaker said: "we need a terminology that tells us we need to dig deeper when we see variants in ClinVar"

Leverage large‑scale multiplexed functional assays (MAVEs) to identify intermediate activity variants | CrisPRO's variant activity modeling can prioritize variants for functional validation | Speaker said: "functional studies... are trying to figure out what these variants are doing"

Apply CrisPRO's computational spine to map intermediate activity scores to predicted cancer risk | CrisPRO can generate calibrated risk models by integrating functional scores with epidemiologic data | Speaker said: "we need quantitative way to do functional analysis and map activity to risk"

Design prospective studies that enroll carriers of intermediate‑activity variants to validate risk predictions | CrisPRO can stratify participants for such trials based on predicted risk tiers | Speaker said: "we lack calibrated thresholds to translate activity into clinical risk"

Develop a computational risk score for Lynch syndrome variants integrating functional, epidemiologic, and polygenic data | CrisPRO can combine variant activity predictions with population risk to generate personalized surveillance recommendations | Speaker said: "we need more variant‑specific cancer risk data"

Create a registry‑based trial that tests extended colonoscopy intervals for carriers of low‑risk MSH6 variants | Use CrisPRO risk tiers to define inclusion criteria and monitor outcomes | Speaker said: "consider extending colonoscopy to the longest interval allowed (every three years) for this variant"

Target BMP1‑driven ECM remodeling to overcome anti‑PD‑1 resistance | CrisPRO can model BMP1‑mediated collagen cross‑linking networks and predict combinatorial inhibition strategies that restore T‑cell access | Speaker said: Blocking BMP1 in combination with anti‑PD‑1 can sensitize resistant tumors to therapy.

Develop BMP1 plasma levels as a predictive biomarker for ICI response | CrisPRO can integrate longitudinal plasma proteomics with tumor‑microenvironment models to define BMP1 thresholds correlating with response | Speaker said: In head‑and‑neck SCC patients, almost all showed higher BMP1 after immunotherapy, but sample size was small and predictive value unclear.

Leverage CrisPRO’s enzyme‑inhibitor payload design to create next‑generation ADCs with optimized linker chemistry for BMP1 inhibition | CrisPRO can simulate linker‑payload stability and predict pharmacokinetic improvements for ADC optimization | Speaker said: Current ADC uses a short‑half‑life BMP1 inhibitor requiring daily dosing; a more stable conjugate could improve efficacy.

Target ARG1‑driven arginine depletion to restore NK cell function in aged metastatic niches | CrisPRO can simulate arginine metabolism networks and predict combinatorial regimens that pair ARG1 inhibition with NK‑cell activating agents | Speaker said: ARG1 inhibitor CB‑1158 significantly decreased liver colonization and increased NK cell infiltration in aged mice.

Develop plasma ARG1 or SFRP1 levels as age‑adjusted biomarkers to select patients for ARG1‑targeted therapy | CrisPRO can integrate transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to define cutoff values for ARG1‑high versus ARG1‑low cohorts | Speaker said: ARG1 was dramatically increased in aged lung fibroblasts and correlated with poorer survival in TCGA melanoma patients over 55.

Combine ARG1 inhibition with NK‑cell checkpoint blockade (e.g., anti‑TIGIT) to synergistically enhance anti‑metastatic immunity in elderly patients | CrisPRO can model dual inhibition of metabolic (ARG1) and checkpoint pathways to forecast additive efficacy | Speaker said: ARG1 treatment increased PD1 and TIGIT expression on NK cells, indicating a checkpoint‑driven exhaustion phenotype.

FGFR2 amplification is enriched in primary tumors of patients who later develop peritoneal metastasis, suggesting a targetable biomarker not currently used for site‑specific therapy. | CrisPRO could integrate spatial transcriptomics and FGFR2 copy‑number data to develop a predictive model for peritoneal spread and guide FGFR‑targeted intraperitoneal therapy. | Speaker said: FGFR2 has been showing more amplified in this peritoneum or the peritoneal mets patients.

High fibroblast and CAF activity creates a physical barrier; targeting CAF‑mediated ECM could improve drug penetration. | CrisPRO can model CAF‑ECM networks to identify synergistic anti‑fibrotic agents to combine with intraperitoneal chemotherapy. | Speaker said: fibroblasts are increased in peritoneal lesions and create dense ECM that blocks drug delivery.

CMS4 molecular subtype predicts poor outcome and may respond differently to intraperitoneal agents. | CrisPRO can develop a CMS‑based classifier to select patients for tailored intraperitoneal therapies (e.g., mitomycin C vs oxaliplatin). | Speaker said: CMS4 subtype is enriched in colorectal peritoneal metastases and has poorer prognosis.

Targeting stromal/TGF‑β pathways could sensitize CMS4 tumors to intraperitoneal chemotherapy. | CrisPRO can model TGF‑β inhibition combined with HIPEC to predict synergistic effects. | Speaker said: CMS4 shows TGF‑beta activation and stromal infiltration.

Targeting the suppressed cGAS‑STING pathway in genome‑doubled tumors could restore immune activation. | CrisPRO can predict which genome‑doubled clones retain residual STING activity and prioritize STING agonists for combination therapy. | Speaker said: high genome doubling leads to down‑regulation of cGAS‑STING signaling despite increased micronucleus formation.

6p HLA loss distinguishes HR‑deficient tumors with high JAK‑STAT signaling; could be used to select patients for immune‑checkpoint blockade. | CrisPRO can integrate single‑cell HLA LOH data with transcriptomics to generate a predictive score for checkpoint inhibitor response. | Speaker said: 6p loss is more common early in BRCA1‑like HRD‑DUP tumors and associates with JAK‑STAT up‑regulation.

SLC7A5 expression is highly up‑regulated in APC‑KRAS tumors and in the squamous subtype of pancreatic cancer, suggesting a patient subset that may benefit from SLC7A5‑targeted strategies. | CrisPRO could develop a transcriptional signature to identify tumors with high SLC7A5 activity for patient selection. | Speaker said: "We found is highly upregulated in the APC KRAS, but it's also highly upregulated under energetic stress."

Combination of STK‑12 with agents that further relieve immunosuppression (e.g., anti‑TGF‑β) may enhance responses in cold tumors. | CrisPRO can simulate multi‑agent synergy on T cell activation pathways. | Speaker highlighted that STK‑12 restores T cell trafficking without classic IL‑2 toxicity.

TLS‑associated immune modules predict PCR; prospective TLS profiling could enrich for responders. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial transcriptomics to predict TLS formation and guide patient selection. | Speaker said: "These subtypes were significantly enriched in treatment‑naive tumors from patients who eventually achieved PCR."

Targeting IL‑17 pathway could rescue patients who develop IRAE‑CNS on checkpoint blockade. | CrisPRO can predict which patients harbor POLR6+ TH17 signatures and prioritize IL‑17 blockade. | Speaker reported improved PET and neurocognitive outcomes with anti‑IL‑17 therapy.

Design a biomarker‑driven trial enrolling VCAN‑low (VPWV) patients and delivering versican via LNP‑mRNA. | CrisPRO can simulate matrix‑immune dynamics to optimize dosing and combination schedules. | Speaker highlighted that versican monotherapy works in VCAN‑low models but requires dual checkpoint blockade in VCAN‑high tumors.

IL-15 superagonist synergizes with anti‑PD‑1 in mouse models, suggesting a combination strategy for pancreatic cancer. | CrisPRO can model the immune‑checkpoint interaction network to predict optimal dosing schedules for IL‑15 + PD‑1 blockade. | Speaker said: "the combination of anti-PD-1 and IL-15 superagonist was really much improved in terms of extending survival relative to each one of these agents alone."

Identify patients with low baseline CD8/IL‑15R signatures who may benefit most from pharmacologic IL‑15 activation. | CrisPRO can integrate transcriptomic and proteomic data to develop a predictive biomarker panel for IL‑15 responsiveness. | Speaker said: "exercise is associated with an increase in just the abundance of the CD8 cells, but also increase in the presence of activated CD8 cells..."

Foghorn's degradation-rate metric lacks integration with patient-specific target half-life biomarkers, presenting an opportunity for CrisPRO to develop predictive models linking degradation kinetics to tumor biomarker profiles. | Use CrisPRO's computational spine to predict optimal degrader dosing regimens based on tumor‑specific protein turnover rates. | Speaker emphasized the need to understand native homeostasis and target half‑lives to interpret degradation‑rate data.

Develop predictive biomarkers for tumors dependent on ARV7 to prioritize patients for the molecular glue therapy. | Use CrisPRO's data integration to correlate ARV7 expression levels with expected degradation efficacy. | Speaker highlighted that ARV7 is present in ~75% of CRPC patients and drives resistance.

Apply CrisPRO to redesign the glue scaffold to engage alternative Cullin‑RING ligases, mitigating potential resistance due to DDB1 loss. | Model alternative E3 recruitment geometries to generate next‑gen glues. | Speaker noted no observed loss of cereblon expression but acknowledged possible ligase pathway alterations.

IRAK kinase inhibitors in clinical trials"

Ancestry‑linked ATM/MGA/SETD2 mutations define a distinct DLBCL subtype that may benefit from repurposed SETD2 inhibitors. | CrisPRO can predict synthetic lethal interactions with SETD2 loss to prioritize combination strategies. | Speaker said: "We are trying to buy the drug back so we can do clinical trials in African Americans who might perhaps benefit from this therapy"

Age‑specific EMT and immune‑checkpoint signatures could be used to stratify patients for tailored therapies. | CrisPRO can integrate transcriptomic EMT scores with clinical outcomes to define age‑adjusted biomarker panels. | Speaker said: "we see an enrichment of EMT‑related genes in older women with triple‑negative breast cancer"

Combine NET inhibition (e.g., PAD4 inhibitors) with standard chemotherapy to reduce necrosis‑driven metastasis. | CrisPRO can predict synergistic drug pairs targeting NET formation and DNA damage pathways. | Speaker demonstrated that disulfiram plus FOLFOX reduced liver metastases in mice.
