text: Neural crest-like tumor cells are protected by SPP1 and post‑N, suggesting a secreted‑factor mediated resistance that could be targeted. | CrisPRO can model secreted factor–receptor networks and predict combinatorial inhibitors to overcome SPP1‑mediated resistance. | Speaker said: "When you add SPP1 to cells, it seems to also protect, only in the neural crest cell line state, it protects cells from interferon and TNF cytokine killing."

Spatially distinct tumor cell states (melanocytic vs neural‑crest) correlate with immune niches, offering a spatial biomarker for patient stratification. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial transcriptomics with outcome data to derive predictive spatial signatures. | Speaker said: "Tumor cells in state one are relatively depleted in immune cells in their neighborhood, and then there's a particular enrichment in T cells in tumor cells with state two."

CSF2 signaling from basal cells is a vulnerability; CrisPRO can design combinatorial inhibitors to disrupt this niche. | CrisPRO can predict synergistic targets downstream of CSF2 to mimic basal‑cell ablation without genetic manipulation. | Speaker said: "CSF2 might be doing something here... removing CSF2 just from the basal cells phenocopies collapsing and killing the basal cells."

SEGER outperforms boundary‑based decontamination methods, offering a more accurate spatial transcriptomics pipeline. | CrisPRO can integrate SEGER‑processed data to improve downstream computational modeling of spatial niches. | Speaker said: "We just say forget the boundary, assign transcripts to cells as link assignment, and that's our big difference."

Targeting OSM‑OSMR signaling together with checkpoint blockade could overcome core‑localized EMT–mediated immunosuppression. | CrisPRO can simulate combined OSM inhibition and immunotherapy to predict synergistic effects on tumor microenvironment. | Speaker said: "Oncostatin M... induces many of the partial EMT genes" and "EMT at the core is associated with lower lymphocyte infiltration."

Spatial EMT pattern (edge vs core) can serve as a predictive biomarker for patient stratification in trials. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial transcriptomics with survival data to develop a spatial EMT signature. | Speaker said: "In some samples, EMT enriched at the edge; in others, EMT enriched at the core... suggests two subtypes of tumors."

The ability to detect multi-marker EV surface signatures offers a new dimension for analyzing liquid biopsies and capturing tumor ecosystem complexity that single analyses cannot resolve. | CrisPRO's computational spine can analyze complex multi-marker signatures from EV surface data to identify novel patient stratification biomarkers. | So overall, we've put together a multimarker profiling technique that we think opens new dimensions for analyzing liquid biopsies. It helps to capture the tumor ecosystem complexity in a way that single analyses can't resolve.

The technology is being expanded to other cancer types beyond colorectal cancer, with potential to decode the composition of the tumor microenvironment based on circulating EVs. | CrisPRO can integrate EV surface signature data with other multi-omic data to provide a comprehensive understanding of the tumor microenvironment across various cancer types. | So we've started working with a few different cancer types, not just colorectal cancer. We're also interested in expanding our library of antibodies to look at the broader tumor microenvironment to kind of decode the composition of that microenvironment based on the circulating EVs.

The spatial organization of B cells and their interactions within niches are predictive of immunotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer, suggesting a gap in current predictive models that primarily focus on T cells or PD-L1. | CrisPRO can leverage spatial multi-omic data to identify and validate B cell-centric biomarkers for immunotherapy response prediction in TNBC. | So taken together, these results from niches, their interactions suggest what drives response to immunotherapy is not just the abundance of B cells but also measures of their spatial organization.

The presence of B cell niches and their interactions, particularly the B activated niche, are associated with immunotherapy response, suggesting that targeting B cell pathways could enhance immunotherapy efficacy. | CrisPRO can analyze the molecular pathways within B cell niches to identify potential combination targets that synergize with immunotherapy. | That specifically the B cell activation signature remains significant across spatial scales, and its interactions are also having predictive capacity for immunotherapy response.

Deep Visual Proteomics can identify early molecular changes in pancreatic precursor lesions and normal ducts associated with cancer development, offering a potential for early detection and stratification. | CrisPRO can integrate DVP-generated proteomic data with genomic and clinical data to build predictive models for PDAC risk stratification and early detection. | And then we had another cohort, which is the cancer-associated cohort, where we isolated cancer-associated normal ducts, low-grade and very rare high-grade PANAs, and the tumor cells.

The ability to combine genotype with phenotype, including KRAS mutations, using DVP, could help in understanding resistance mechanisms to targeted therapies and potentially identify salvage strategies. | CrisPRO can analyze DVP data to identify specific KRAS mutation profiles associated with treatment resistance and suggest combination therapies or alternative treatment strategies. | And just to give you an idea, what we found is that when we look at the ADMs in low-grade, we can see in a number of those hotspot mutations, when we look on the patient level, we can see that some patients have one mutation, others have several different mutations in the different regions of interest.

High stromal CD8 density in ER+ breast cancer is a predictive marker of chemo inferiority and adds prognostic information to clinical variables, suggesting a need for improved patient stratification beyond current genomic assays. | CrisPRO can integrate spatial immune multi-omic data with genomic and clinical data to develop a refined prognostic model for ER+ breast cancer, identifying patients who may not benefit from chemotherapy. | But more crucially is that the inflamed milieu, particularly those with high stromal CD8, at least in alcohol, is a predictive marker of chemo inferiority. It does add significant prognostic information to clinical variables, including menopausal status.

metadata.institution: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland

text: The identification of dysfunctional immune states in ER+ breast cancer, including checkpoint upregulation and M2-like macrophage signatures, suggests potential for combination therapies with immunotherapy. | CrisPRO can analyze the molecular pathways within these dysfunctional immune states to identify novel combination targets that could synergize with immunotherapy in ER+ breast cancer. | The inflamed states do appear transcriptomically wired to more dysfunctions, such as the expression of checkpoints, exhaustion transcripts, M2-like macrophage, and remodeling genes, as well as dedifferentiation, potentially from luminal biology.

metadata.speaker: Zach Kinsella
metadata.institution: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland

text: The platform allows for the identification of novel combination targets by analyzing the phenotypic shifts of CRISPR-edited tumors upon therapeutic intervention, such as identifying a rationale for combining VEGF pathway inhibitors with PD1 blockade. | CrisPRO can leverage the BERTA platform to screen genetic perturbations and therapeutic combinations, identifying synergistic targets and predicting optimal therapeutic strategies. | And so what becomes interesting is that we can look at the trajectories of these different knockouts upon treatment with different drugs. And for example, if you here look at this knockout of VGFR1, the VGFR receptor, when you treat this knockout with PD1, you see a drastic shift towards the right of the space of the phenotype of this tumor. So these tumors under PD1 become tumors that have a very hot TME.

The ability to project human biology onto mouse models allows for the identification of human-specific biomarkers, such as CCAM6, in preclinical settings, which can then be used for patient stratification. | CrisPRO can utilize the humanization capability of the BERTA platform to identify and validate human biomarkers in preclinical models, facilitating their translation to clinical applications. | And what we find that we look at the knockouts, it's a knockout of a transcription factor that essentially is going to induce a switch in histology of the tumor. And the resulting histology resembles the tumor histology in patients that have high CCAM6 expression.

The trial did not use risk‑based biomarkers to prioritize patients for FIT vs FIT‑DNA, creating an opportunity for CrisPRO to develop predictive risk scores to guide test selection. | CrisPRO can generate individualized risk models integrating demographics, insurance status, and prior screening history to assign the optimal stool‑based test, improving yield and cost‑effectiveness. | Speaker noted that "we did not assess cost effectiveness" and that FIT kit brand differences affected positivity rates

Standardize FIT kit brand and incorporate real‑time colonoscopy capacity data to reduce variability across sites. | CrisPRO’s simulation engine can model site‑specific logistics and suggest optimal kit selection and navigation intensity per clinic. | Speaker said "different FIT kit brands with different positivity rates" and "colonoscopies were limited despite navigation"

CrisPRO can incorporate real‑time scan results and comorbidity weighting to improve algorithm precision for minority patients. | CrisPRO’s dynamic data integration layer can ingest EMR imaging feeds instantly, updating eligibility matches on the fly. | Speaker noted that timing of scan results was a major limitation for the algorithm

Provide a unified, AI‑driven trial‑matching platform that reduces manual review by >35% and improves eligibility capture. | CrisPRO’s scalable matching engine can handle larger trial catalogs and patient cohorts with higher accuracy. | Speaker reported that the current algorithm reduced manual review by 35% but still missed many eligible patients

Partner with CrisPRO to embed zip‑code based risk modeling and AI‑driven mobile unit routing to extend screening reach. | CrisPRO can generate geospatial risk maps and optimize mobile unit deployment schedules. | Speaker highlighted need for mobile vans and mentioned zip‑code level disparities

Combine NET‑targeting (e.g., DNase or PAD4 inhibitors) with glucocorticoid receptor antagonists to prevent stress‑induced metastatic niche formation | CrisPRO can simulate synergistic effects of NET inhibition plus GR blockade on metastatic outgrowth | Speaker said: "DNase treatment reduced metastasis in the lungs of the stressed animals, almost back to background level"

Identify patients with high circulating NET markers or neutrophil activation as those who may be harmed by glucocorticoid therapy | CrisPRO can integrate NET‑derived biomarkers with patient stress profiles to stratify risk | Speaker said: "glucocorticoid receptor knockout in neutrophils abolished stress‑induced NET formation and metastasis"

Develop blood‑based NET or inflammatory gene signatures that correlate with epigenetic age acceleration and social stressors | CrisPRO can integrate multi‑omic stress signatures to refine risk stratification beyond socioeconomic indices | Speaker highlighted that tobacco use and BMI were strong drivers of epigenetic age acceleration

Design prospective cohort with repeated epigenetic clock measurements and detailed glucocorticoid exposure to capture temporal dynamics | CrisPRO can model optimal sampling intervals and power calculations for epigenetic aging endpoints | Speaker noted need for larger samples and more repeated measures to assess trajectories

Need for biomarkers to predict which tumors are dependent on KAT2A versus KAT2B, enabling patient selection for selective degraders | CrisPRO can integrate proteomic dependency data with structural predictions to define a KAT2A‑dependency signature | Speaker said: "in paralog screening data ... most of the activity really comes from the A component"

PK challenges of the KAT2A degrader could be addressed by redesign using CrisPRO‑guided scaffold optimization | CrisPRO predicts how small‑molecule modifications affect degrader‑induced ternary complex stability and pharmacokinetic properties | Speaker said: "These compounds still have some PK challenges, so we didn't quite fully cover the target"

Extending the degradomics pipeline to non‑cereblon E3 ligases where CrisPRO can model novel ternary interfaces | CrisPRO’s computational spine can generate predictive models for any E3‑ligase substrate receptor given structural inputs | Speaker said: "we have similar data on other ligases. HR1047R mutation drives helix‑12 swinging; CrisPRO can model how this mutation stabilizes the active conformation for targeted inhibitor design | Predictive modeling of mutant‑specific conformational ensembles to design molecules that re‑stabilize the inactive state | Speaker said: "the histidine 1047 mutation ... allows swinging of the helix and adopting this active conformation"

Differential dependence on RTK versus RAS recruitment suggests a need for mutation‑specific biomarkers | Integrate structural activation states with phosphoproteomic signatures to define patient subsets | Speaker said: "the helical domain mutations retain pretty high dependency on phosphorylated RTKs"

Incorporate membrane‑mimetic nanodisc assays into early‑phase trials to select compounds that achieve full membrane‑engaged activation blockade | CrisPRO can simulate compound effects on membrane‑bound conformations to prioritize candidates before clinical testing | Speaker said: "we used lipid nanodiscs to reconstitute the active complex"

CrisPRO can computationally predict low‑populated kinase conformations, complementing NMR and accelerating hit identification | CrisPRO’s conformational ensemble modeling can generate virtual libraries targeting the same invisible pockets identified by NMR | Speaker said: "we can now design selective inhibitors for this state"

Apply the invisible‑state targeting approach to kinases implicated in resistant cancers where current inhibitors fail | Use CrisPRO to map invisible states across the kinome and match them to disease‑specific mutation profiles | Speaker said: "Gleevec binds very selectively to this low populated state"

Quantitative BAFF‑R expression thresholds could identify patients most likely to benefit from the BAFF‑R CAR | CrisPRO can integrate flow cytometry and transcriptomic data to define a BAFF‑R expression score for patient selection | Speaker noted uncertainty about antigen density and its impact on CAR efficacy

Combine CD19 CAR with BAFF‑R CAR (bispecific) to prevent antigen‑loss relapse in ALL | CrisPRO can model synergistic killing dynamics of dual‑target CARs and predict optimal dosing ratios | Speaker mentioned development of a bispecific CAR expressing both Baff‑CAR and CD19 scFv

Target the TGF‑β–driven transcriptional program (e.g., Aeolus) with CrisPRO‑derived small‑molecule modulators to restore T cell function without inducing apoptosis | CrisPRO can predict transcription factor modulators that selectively dampen TGF‑β‑induced Aeolus activity while preserving survival pathways | Speaker identified a dominant TGF‑β signature and Aeolus as a key regulator of dysfunction

Leverage CrisPRO’s ability to design high‑affinity, methylation‑insensitive TCRs for KRAS G12V, overcoming epitope heterogeneity | CrisPRO can model post‑translational modifications and redesign TCR CDR loops for consistent binding to both methylated and unmethylated peptides | Speaker described methylation of the KRAS G12V epitope causing variable TCR recognition

Combine engineered CD4 helper cells with costimulatory fusion receptors to sustain CD8 TCR function in solid tumors | CrisPRO can predict optimal CD4‑CD8 pairing and fusion receptor designs to maximize synergistic anti‑tumor activity | Speaker showed that CD4 help restored CD8 persistence and that fusion receptors can provide costimulation

Functional HRD assays (e.g., RAD51 foci, STRIDE) could better select patients who will benefit from high‑trap PARP inhibitors. | CrisPRO can integrate functional HRD signatures with genomic data to predict PARP trapping dependency. | RAD51 foci expression indicating reactivation of HR in non‑responders; >90% of resistant models show RAD51 foci.

Combine high‑trap PARP inhibitors with agents that prevent HR re‑activation (e.g., POLQ inhibitors) to overcome resistance. | CrisPRO can model synthetic lethal networks to prioritize POLQ as a partner for PARP inhibition. | Resistant clones lost ability to trap PARP; loss of trapping correlated with resistance.

Use CrisPRO to redesign ARID1B binders to eliminate hook effect and improve degradation kinetics. | Computational protein‑ligand modeling can predict off‑target interactions and guide redesign. | Hook effect observed with cereblon‑based molecule; need for better potency/selectivity.

Identify synergistic partners for SMARCA2 inhibition (e.g., ATR inhibitors) using synthetic lethal network analysis. | CrisPRO can map dependencies in BRG1‑deficient tumors to prioritize rational combos. | SMARCA2 inhibition combined with PD‑1 blockade showed complete responses in mouse model.

PSMA PET intensity alone does not fully predict response; integrating FDG PET or dynamic SUV kinetics could improve patient selection for lutetium‑based RPT. | CrisPRO can model multimodal imaging signatures (PSMA + FDG) to predict therapeutic response and guide eligibility thresholds. | Speaker noted that "30% of patients did not respond or were resistant" and highlighted low PSMA uptake and FDG discordance as possible reasons.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Zach Morris
metadata.session_title: Targeted Alpha and Beta Emitting Radiopharmaceuticals: Multidisciplinary Precision Radiation Medicine

text: NEO811 shows activity in acquired resistance to HIF-2 alpha inhibitors (G323E mutation) and intrinsic resistance (low HIF-2 alpha, high HIF-1 alpha). | CrisPRO's platform can identify pan-HIF activity and its implications in resistance settings, potentially guiding combination strategies. | NEO811 still retained full activity [in G323E mutation model]... NEO811 showed robust tumor growth inhibition, and again, a little bit better than just HIF-2 alpha alone. Again, these PDXs, they're serially transplanted over time. So we're doing the PD assessment on these, and they may now express a little HIF-2 compared to the publication, because again, belzutifan did show some activity. But we're very excited because NEO811 not only shows activity in acquired resistance to HIF-2 alpha inhibitors, but also intrinsic resistance, showing this pan-HIF activity may really be a driver in the clinic.

NEO811 shows combination effect with belzutifan and potential for combinations with other standards of care. | CrisPRO can analyze synergistic effects of NEO811 with other standards of care, identifying optimal combination partners for CRCC. | So even though we are encouraged as the single agent studies, we wanted to then go in and say, can we do anything with combinations with other standard of cares, really to hit these pathways a little bit harder? And so giving the clinical success of HIF-2 alpha inhibitors, especially belzutifan recently, we wanted to test NEO811 and belzutifan in combination... not only adding a HIF-2 alpha inhibitor with ARNT, so they're targeting the exact same pathway, is that hopefully in the future, this will open us up to other combinations of other standards of care.

While CCNE1 amplification is a strong biomarker, some amplified cell lines show reduced sensitivity, potentially due to P16 expression or other factors. | CrisPRO can analyze the interplay of CCNE1 amplification, P16 expression, and CDK4/6 activity to refine patient stratification for MRT55811. | Yes. So one interesting phenomenon is that cyclin E1 amplified cancers are almost always P16 high, so they express an endogenous inhibitor of CDK4/6. So it appears that, and there's also evidence for that, that there is a downside of having both hyperactive CDK2 and active CDK4/6 on top of it. So it's either/or in most cases. There was, I think in this panel, two exceptions, which had low P16, and this explains that then CDK4/6 is active at the same time as CDK2 and pure cyclin E1 degradation doesn't work.

The CCNE1 degrader shows activity in models resistant to CDK2 inhibitors, suggesting a potential to overcome resistance to existing therapies. | CrisPRO can identify patient populations that have failed or are resistant to CDK2 inhibitors but may benefit from CCNE1 degradation. | CDK2 inhibitors, interestingly, are a bit different. So they do show preferential activity for cyclin E1 amplified cell lines, and that's more obvious in the lower plot where you can see the GI50s. But there are significant overlaps, so there's also a lot of activity in cell lines that are not amplified. We have seen this with multiple CDK2 inhibitors, not all are shown here.

HuR dependency is strongly correlated with BRAF mutations, suggesting BRAF mutant CRC as a key indication, but other BRAF mutant cancers may also be sensitive. | CrisPRO can analyze the correlation between HuR dependency and BRAF mutations across various cancer types to identify additional indications for HuR degraders. | Analysis of that data showed a strong and positive correlation between HUR dependency and BRAF. Since BRAF mutations are prevalent in skin and colorectal cancers, we suppose that a BRAF mutant colorectal cancer might be particularly sensitive to HUR degradation.

HuR degrader shows comparable efficacy to BRAF inhibitors in BRAF-mutant CRC, including dabrafenib-resistant models, suggesting it can overcome or bypass resistance. | CrisPRO can identify patients with BRAF-mutant CRC who have developed resistance to BRAF inhibitors and may benefit from HuR degradation therapy. | BRAF dabrafenib-resistant MDSDN cells were generated through long-time exposure. As expected, these resistant cells showed a clear loss of sensitivity to dabrafenib compared with this parental compound. In contrast, when treated with our HUR degrader Both parental compound and dabrafenib-resistant cells displayed strong and comparable reductions in cell viabilities.

The HuR degrader induces interferon signaling, suggesting potential for combination with immune-oncology therapies. | CrisPRO can analyze the immune-modulatory effects of HuR degraders and identify synergistic combinations with immunotherapies. | This increase in interferon signaling then leads to increased secretion of chemokines and cytokines. In this model, we can see an increase in CCL5 and CXCL10, which of course, are important chemoattractants for T cells in the tumor microenvironment.

BB010203 shows strong combination potential with HER2-targeted agents (tucatinib, trastuzumab) in HER2-amplified models, potentially overcoming shortcomings of existing therapies. | CrisPRO can analyze the synergistic effects of BB010203 with HER2-targeted agents and other therapies in HER2-amplified cancers to optimize combination strategies. | So to test that in BT474 cell lines, which is a HER2-amplified model, we gave the combined approach of 10203 in combination with tucatinib here on the left or trastuzumab here on the right. And what you can see in blue is strong monotherapy effects with 10203. But when you combine that with the other agent, it led to strong regressions... And when given in combination with the HER2 targeting antibody trastuzumab, led to strong regressions, and again, outperformed the combination of tucatinib plus trastuzumab.

The disruption of non-canonical RAS signaling by BB010203 may address resistance mechanisms to canonical RAS inhibitors and HER2-targeted therapies. | CrisPRO can identify resistance mechanisms to HER2-targeted therapies and canonical RAS inhibitors that are driven by non-canonical RAS signaling, and assess BB010203's potential to overcome them. | So this data shows by genetic mechanisms that the PIK3CA RAS interaction is essential for phospho-AKT activation and survival. So to understand what RAS isoforms were driving this dependency, the first thing we did is we screened our panel of our two amplified lines against with 10203 compared to the pan-RAS inhibitor 6236. And what we observed is that with 10203, as expected, we saw complete phospho-AKT suppression. But with the pan-RAS inhibitor RMC-6236, we saw moderate suppression of phospho-AKT, despite seeing complete phospho-ERK suppression. This was seen across a larger panel of lines, here shown on the right. So this data to us indicated that the phospho-AKT activity in these lines was not likely driven from canonical RAS proteins, which were inhibited by the RMC-6236, but likely coming from non-canonical proteins, which were not hit by 6236.

KAT2 inhibition upregulates interferon responses, suggesting potential for combination with immune-oncology therapies like BCMA CD3 bispecific antibodies. | CrisPRO can analyze the immune-modulatory effects of KAT2 inhibitors and identify synergistic combinations with T-cell engagers and other immunotherapies. | So we then utilized a mouse syngeneic model of multiple myeloma to test tumor growth inhibition in combination with BCMA CD3 bispecific antibody. ... But additionally, what you can see also is that we do extend the tumor growth delay in a dose-dependent manner when we add our KAT2 inhibitor with the bispecific antibody. And this is reflected in the survival curve shown on the right. So we're very excited about the idea that this could potentially open up opportunities to combine our KAT2 inhibitor with IO therapies to deepen responses in multiple myeloma.

KAT2 inhibition shows synergistic activity with IMiDs (lenalidomide, pomalidomide) in multiple myeloma, suggesting it can enhance the efficacy of standard of care treatments. | CrisPRO can identify patient populations with multiple myeloma who may benefit from combination therapy with KAT2 inhibitors and IMiDs. | So we combined our KAT2 inhibitor with either lenalidomide or pomalidomide in a combination matrix experiment for proliferation in vitro. ... So when you get this output data, if you get a value between zero to one, this is considered additive, and you can see this by the column on the right where we have the self-cross of our compound with itself and those values range there. If you have a value that's greater than one, this suggests you can have synergy between the two compounds, and you can see for both our KAT2 inhibitor combination with lenalidomide and pomalidomide, most of the cell lines we observe synergistic scores.

The SAGA complex and KAT2A/B are identified as top dependencies for multiple myeloma, suggesting a potential for biomarker-driven patient selection. | CrisPRO can analyze the dependency of various cancer types on SAGA and KAT2A/B to identify optimal indications and biomarkers for KAT2 inhibitors. | So what you're seeing here is this is a bit of the DepMap data where we were asking in multiple myeloma cells versus every other tumor type, what are the protein complexes that myeloma cells are most dependent on? And so we used the CRISPR dropout scores here. We used a quorum protein complex analysis, and what you can see here is that the SAGA complex and other KAT2-containing complexes showed up as the top dependencies for multiple myeloma, as are highlighted here in the red.

RMO-55 demonstrates activity in models of acquired resistance to RAS on inhibitors, particularly those involving KRAS amplification or increased expression. | CrisPRO can identify resistance mechanisms to RAS inhibitors, including those involving RAS amplification or overexpression, and assess RMO-55's potential to overcome them. | So going back to the clinical resistance I started with, one of the major mechanisms of clinical resistance, at least in terms of where we can detect a mechanism of resistance from genomic alterations in ctDNA, is KRAS amplification of the mutant associated with the G12 mutant allele... However, RMO-55 at 10 MPK was able to produce deep and very durable regressions in these resistant models. In a related model, we looked at the ability of RMO-55 to restore tumor control in tumors that were already outgrowing on deraxone rasib. And you can see here, these tumors initially showed regression, but then started to grow out with continued deraxone rasib treatment. However, in the group that we switched over to RMO-55, we were able to restore tumor control and had durable regressions out to the end of the study.

RMO-55's catalytic mechanism and potential for broader RAS inhibition suggest opportunities for combination with other RAS inhibitors or therapies targeting downstream effectors. | CrisPRO can analyze the synergistic effects of RMO-55 with RAS-off inhibitors and other therapies targeting the RAS pathway to optimize combination strategies. | So the G13 and some of the Q61, we have steric occlusion activity analogous to the steric occlusion activity that I described at wild type. Demonstrate computational advantage of circRNA stability over linear mRNA for sustained cytokine expression. | Model kinetic profiles to optimize dosing schedules. | Speaker showed kinetic advantage of circRNA versus mRNA in vitro and in vivo.

Develop a predictive model of TAM receptor density to select patients most likely to benefit. | Integrate IHC quantification data with transcriptomics to generate a TAM‑score. | Speaker emphasized that more TAMs = better efficacy.

Develop a predictive model of intratumoral collagen I/III levels to select patients for CBD anti‑CTLA‑4 therapy. | Integrate RNA‑seq and imaging data to generate a collagen‑score. | Speaker highlighted collagen I/III up‑regulation in recurrent GBM.

CrisPRO could suggest synergistic checkpoint combinations (e.g., CBD PD‑1) to enhance efficacy. | Model immune network effects of dual collagen‑binding checkpoints. | Speaker discussed potential to combine with PD‑1/PD‑L1 blockade.

CrisPRO can model DLL3 down‑regulation and suggest alternative co‑stimulatory domains. | Simulate antigen loss scenarios and predict efficacy of CD2 co‑stimulation. | Speaker noted that tarlatamab loses activity over serial challenges while trispecific retains.

Incorporate DLL3 expression biomarker thresholds into early‑phase trial design. | Optimize inclusion criteria using predictive modeling of DLL3 prevalence. | Speaker emphasized need for DLL3‑positive tumors for activity.

CrisPRO can integrate copy‑number and exome data to derive a predictive HR‑deficiency score for the combination. | Machine‑learning model to predict synergy based on genomic alterations. | Speaker highlighted copy‑number gain/loss differences between responders and non‑responders.

Suggest rational addition of immune checkpoint blockade to exploit increased mutational load from DNA repair inhibition. | Simulate tumor‑immune interactions under combined DDR and checkpoint inhibition. | Speaker asked about combining with checkpoint inhibition.

Use CrisPRO to integrate 3D model drug response data with patient genomic profiles for adaptive trial enrichment. | Predict which patient sub‑cohorts will align with 3D model sensitivity patterns. | Speaker emphasized need for better preclinical models to improve confidence.

Repurpose cathepsin inhibitors (e.g., E64d) to block extracellular matrix remodeling downstream of legumen loss | CrisPRO can assess off‑target effects of cathepsin inhibitors in AML microenvironment | Speaker said: "added the E64d inhibitor, which rescued the collagen degradation phenotype"

Design trials that stratify by patient age and stromal SFRP1 levels to avoid signal dilution seen in mixed‑age cohorts | CrisPRO can simulate age‑stratified enrollment scenarios to optimize statistical power | Speaker emphasized that age dramatically alters metastasis kinetics

Incorporate collagen I quantification or MR elastography as stratification biomarkers in trials of agents targeting copy number variation (e.g., PARP inhibitors, DNA repair modulators). | CrisPRO can simulate trial arms with and without stiffness‑based enrichment to estimate power gains. | Speaker said: "collagen I correlates with CNV across TCGA cancers"

Identify tumors where CCR8+ Treg depletion fails due to alternative suppressive pathways. | CrisPRO can model compensatory immunosuppressive networks beyond CCR8. | Speaker admitted that "we have not seen a specific signal with SD either" and that efficacy was limited.
